passage:
The onboarding room at the logistics firm had a bowl of mints and a stack of contracts. Parul from HR smiled. "Sign at the flags, and you're all set."

Vasudha loved the company. The interviews had been warm, and she wanted to say yes before anyone changed their mind. She picked up the pen.

Then she remembered a cousin's story about a bond nobody had read. She put the pen down. "May I take twenty minutes with this first?"

"Of course," Parul said. "Most people do."

Vasudha read the notice period, the clause about outside work, the ownership of anything she made, and a training bond. She underlined the bond and asked, "How long does it apply, and what happens if I leave earlier?"

Parul explained it plainly. Vasudha asked about the outside-work clause too, then signed. Her hand felt steadier than before.

qa.q: What was in the bowl on the table in the onboarding room?
qa.a: There was a bowl of mints on the table.

qa.q: Why did Vasudha pick up the pen so quickly at first?
qa.a: Vasudha loved the company and wanted to say yes before anyone changed their mind, so trust made her want to sign fast.

qa.q: What did Vasudha do that made trust safer?
qa.a: Vasudha read the notice period, outside-work clause, ownership clause and bond, and asked questions about the bond before signing.

qa.q: How might Parul feel about Vasudha's questions?
qa.a: Parul says most people take time to read, so Parul probably sees careful readers as normal and good for the company, not as a sign of distrust.

grounding: Vasudha trusts the company and wants to sign fast, then reads notice, non-compete, ownership and bond clauses and asks questions.

passage:
I'm Dolma, and I almost signed my first real job contract in ten minutes. The design studio in Gangtok felt like home: kind people, plants everywhere, Irawati from HR handing me tea. I trusted them completely.
Then my friend Karma said, "Read it. All of it. Even if you love them."
So I took it home. Page six had a two-year bond with a penalty if I left early. Page eight said every design I made, even on weekends, belonged to the studio. And the notice period was three months, not one, as I'd been told.
I felt a bit silly, but I emailed Irawati five questions. She replied the next day: the bond could come down to one year, weekend personal work could be excluded, and the notice was a typo.
Looking back, she didn't mind at all. She said, "Good. I like people who read."

qa.q: What did page eight of the contract say?
qa.a: That every design Dolma made, even on weekends, belonged to the studio.

qa.q: How did Dolma feel about questioning the contract?
qa.a: Dolma felt a bit silly and awkward, because of trusting the studio completely.

qa.q: What was wise about Dolma's approach?
qa.a: Dolma read every clause, including the bond, penalty, IP and notice period, and asked clear questions before signing.

qa.q: How might Irawati see Dolma's five questions?
qa.a: Irawati seems pleased and respectful, seeing a careful reader rather than a difficult one.

grounding: The protagonist trusts the company and wants to sign fast, but reads the bond, penalty, IP and notice clauses and asks questions; a good employer welcomes it.

passage:
Mentor's note, Tuesday.
Mahima called me from the lobby of the Mumbai hospital group, pen in hand, ready to sign her new contract as a clinic manager. She said, "They're lovely people, Reena-ma'am. I trust them." I asked her to read it to me before signing.
She sounded uncomfortable, but did. There was a two-year service bond with a penalty for leaving early. There was a non-compete stopping her from working at any clinic in the city for a year after leaving. The notice period was ninety days.
She went quiet. I told her trust was fine, but paper decides. I suggested she ask HR to explain the non-compete and bond in writing, and consider asking a lawyer friend to look at it.
She asked HR for a day to review. They agreed without fuss. She called me that evening, relieved, with three questions ready for them. A fair employer is happy to wait for a careful reader.

qa.q: How long was the non-compete in Mahima's contract?
qa.a: A year after leaving, covering any clinic in the city.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling as she read the contract aloud?
qa.a: She felt uncomfortable at first, then went quiet as the clauses worried her, and later felt relieved to take time.
Asking HR to explain the non-compete and bond in writing, considering a lawyer friend's review, and not signing in a hurry.

qa.q: How might the HR team see Mahima's request for a day?
qa.a: They seem to see it as normal and reasonable, which is why they agreed without fuss.

grounding: The protagonist trusts the employer and wants to sign quickly; a mentor helps her read the bond, non-compete and notice clauses and ask questions.
